Understanding clinical trials

Clinical trials are research studies in people. Today’s standard treatments exist because earlier patients joined trials. Trials are available at every stage of cancer, not only when other treatments have stopped working.

The phases

  • Phase 1A small group. Finds a safe dose and studies side effects.
  • Phase 2More people. Looks at whether the treatment works against a certain cancer, while continuing to watch safety.
  • Phase 3Often hundreds or thousands of people. Compares the new treatment with the current standard treatment.
  • Phase 4After approval. Gathers more information on long-term benefits and side effects.

Treatments tested in phase 1 and 2 trials are investigational: promising, but not yet proven. Results from early trials can change as more people are studied.

Your protections

  • Before you join, the team must explain the study in a language you understand and get your written informed consent.
  • You can leave a trial at any time, for any reason, and still receive care.
  • Placebos (inactive pills) are rarely used alone in cancer treatment trials. Usually one group gets the standard treatment and another gets the standard or the new treatment being studied.
  • In randomized trials, neither you nor your doctor chooses which group you are in.

Costs

The study sponsor often pays for the study drug and study-only tests. Many health plans cover routine care during a qualifying trial. Ask the study team exactly what you or your insurance would pay, and about help with travel.

How to look for a trial

  • Ask your oncologist first: “Is there a clinical trial that fits my cancer and stage?”
  • Search ClinicalTrials.gov by cancer type and city.
  • Call the National Cancer Institute’s Cancer Information Service: 1-800-4-CANCER (1-800-422-6237), with help in English and Spanish.
